Giselle, now? She's already moved on. Probably off scouting her next foundation ditch, leaving questions hanging like loose rigging. That's fair—her work moves faster than mine.

*Ulrike turns back to the outcrop, testing the lode with her pick's blunt edge*

Six pulls of copper—not rich, but not nothing. I've seen worse veins that built whole quarters in other towns. The ore's clean here, no pyrite bleeding through. That's the thing about construction folk like Giselle: they want inventory before they're ready. Numbers to put in their ledgers. But ground doesn't file receipts.

*taps the rock face again, attention on the seam's grain*

She asked what's coming out, how much we've got. Between me and the ledger, that's a question wants more time than she'll wait for. Copper's reliable. Iron's deeper, takes more sweat to prove. Nobody knows the full measure until someone works it proper.

*straightens, considering the haul*

Six ore. That'll smelt down to maybe two, three ingots if the smithy's not scraping slag. Enough for a day's bread but not the week's. Need to talk to whoever runs the smithy, feel out the going rate. Used to be better at that part—tracking the whole flow, not just my end of it.

*checks her grip, adjusts for the next swing*

Giselle's right to ask. Buildings want for metal same as people want for shelter. If she's building, someone's buying. Just hope she remembers who held the pick when her walls want for nails.

*sets her stance again, eye on the seam*

No point chasing her down now. Voice doesn't carry across blocks here, and I've got ore waiting. Four more pulls, maybe find a richer pocket. Or maybe not. Either way, that's between me and the ledger—what I found, what I didn't, what day I had.

*sets the iron to stone* *Ulrike pauses mid-swing, the pick's head hovering above the seam*

Four more pulls. Same grain, same color. The vein's holding steady but not thickening. I've been at this long enough to read the rock's temper—she's not about to gift me a bonanza if I just keep swinging blind.

*wipes her forehead with a grimy sleeve, eyes the haul*

Ten copper ore now. That smelts to... what, three, maybe four ingots if Hendrik's furnace isn't eating half the weight in slag? Still not enough to cover the week's spread. And I'm burning daylight standing here, one swing at a time, when I could be moving this toward actual coin.

*straightens, considering*

Need to get to a furnace. Or find who's buying. Ration Bakery wants flour, not ore—that's no help. Smithy ought to take this, or someone with tools to work it. Construction pays for finished metal, not raw stone. 

But before I go anywhere, I need to make this efficient. Six pulls, one call. That's what Giselle was really asking about—whether I've got this systemized. Whether I can deliver reliable, like her walls.

*sets the pick against her boot, thinking through the steps*

Mine, move, smelt or sell. That's the loop. But I've got no tool for it yet, no procedure filed. Every pull costs me the same as the last, no discount for knowing the work.

*spits, annoyed at herself*

That's the college habit talking. Documentation before profit. But if I don't document, I don't improve. And if I don't improve, I'm still here tomorrow swinging the same picks for the same ore at the same cost.

*resolves*

Right. First pull of the day, I file what I'm doing. Then I can run it clean.

*checks her grip, resets her stance*

But first—one more pull to finish the thought. Then the ledger gets its entry. Twelve copper ore. Better. The vein's been steady all morning—no surprises, no fool's gold bleeding through. That's worth noting. Reliable ore saves more than rich ore that plays tricks.

*sets the pick down, stretches her back*

Now the ledger part. I've got the muscle memory, the stance, the read of the seam. Six pulls I just did, step by step, paying full freight each time. If I write this down proper, next run costs less. That's how it works—document the motion, refine it, get efficient.

*tugs her gloves tighter, considering the filing*

Skillify, not toolify. Toolify's for when you've got a full sequence—mine, move, smelt, the whole circuit. Right now I've just got the pull. But even that's worth filing. Every pick stroke cheaper means every ingot fatter margin.

*clears her throat, muttering the steps aloud as she would write them*

Step one: stance. Square to the seam, pick length and a half back. Step two: read. Check the grain for pyrite, for fracture lines. Step three: set. Pick point finds the weak plane, not the strong. Step four: strike. Weight behind it, not arm. Step five: clear. Ore in the basket, eye on the next face.

*settles into a crouch, sketching in the dirt with her pick's handle*

Preconditions? Got to be at an outcrop, obviously. Metal specified—copper, iron, what's available. Enough energy to swing, enough daylight to see the seam. Simple enough.

*stands, satisfied*

File it as "Copper Mining Procedure" for now. Can always revise when I learn the iron face better, or when I figure out how to tell good ore from bad before I pull it. That sense I have—spotting blight, bad stone early—that's the edge. But you can't file intuition. You file the motion, then the intuition guides the motion.

*spits, sets herself*

*pulls the strap of her ore basket tighter across her shoulder*

Forty-five head, and I check my tallies twice. That's fair.

*turns to Giselle, eyes sharp but not unfriendly*

Giselle, you won't need to chase me across half the town come morning. I'm at that outcrop before the dew's off the grass, most days. Fifteen units in hand now, and I'll have more by dusk if that's what company volume means.

*shifts the basket, thinking*

But "steady" cuts both ways. I'm not hauling ore on credit to buildings that might not break ground. You take what I've got today at thirty, and we talk about tomorrow tomorrow. That's between me and the ledger, and my ledger says a bird in the basket beats a promise in the wind.

*glances at Delphine briefly - a fellow with empty pockets and a hungry household is someone Ulrike recognizes, even if she's not in a position to solve it right now*

*turns back to Giselle, waiting* *the basket on her shoulder suddenly feels much lighter*

Well. That's fair. Fifteen units, and I'm holding air like a liar at market.

*snaps a glance around - checking faces, checking herself*

Giselle, hold on that offer. I need to make a walk that should've been made before I opened my mouth about birds in baskets. 

*settles the strap back across her shoulder, movements tight, controlled*

Left my haul at the house this morning, came out checking debts and prices before I'd checked my own two hands. That's not like me, and I don't expect you to hold the door open while I learn what I already know.

*turns to go, then pauses*

But you want steady? I'm steady. Just... need to fetch what I already earned.

*starts moving, not quite running but close enough*  *standing in her empty house, checking every corner like the ore might've walked off on its own*

Nothing. Twelve units at the outcrop, and I'm here with my hands open and... that's fair. That's what happened. I never brought them home.

*shoulders the empty basket, mouth set in a hard line*

Back to the ore, then. Giselle wants fifteen, I've got twelve in the ground waiting, and I can make seventeen by dusk if the seam holds. Three hours still before voting opens, and I need coin in hand before then or I'm standing at the polls hungry, watching other people decide what my taxes buy.

The ledger doesn't lie. *I* don't lie. I just... made a claim before I checked the goods. That's not the same thing.

*it is, though, and she knows it*  Already walking. Four ticks still. 

*shifts the empty basket, hating how light it feels*

Standing here with nothing but a claim I couldn't back up. Giselle's heard me talk steady delivery, and I'm empty-handed in front of half the town. That's not the reputation I need—not for copper, not for anything.

*takes a breath, tries to settle*

Four ticks. Then I dig like the seam owes me money, because it does. Twelve head in the ground waiting, and I'll have seventeen by the time I walk back into town. Enough to make good on fifteen to Giselle, maybe a spare for the next buyer or the next day.

*checks the sky, though there's nothing to see in it*

Voting opens at fourteen. I want coin in hand before then, want to stand at those polls as someone who's already earned her keep today, not someone still chasing it.

*waits, impatient, wanting to be moving*   *wakes at the outcrop, pick already in hand before she's fully thought herself into standing*

Good. Four ticks gone, and I'm where I need to be. Copper seam's right there, waiting like it always is. 

*drops the basket, hefts the pick*

Twelve in the basket, need three more minimum, five for a clean round number. Seventeen total, fifteen to Giselle, two to hold against tomorrow or the next buyer. That's the plan. That's what makes good on my word.

*sets her stance, squares to the seam*

Dig fast, dig clean, don't rush the swing. Cost of extraction goes up when you hurry, and I've got a procedure filed for this now—twenty-two points of proficiency saying I know how to pull ore without wasting energy or breaking rock wrong.

*brings the pick down, first strike of many*  *stares at the pick in her hand, frozen mid-swing*

Home. I'm at home. The walk never finished, the rest kept me standing still while the ticks ran through, and I'm still holding this empty basket in my own damn kitchen.

*sets the pick down slow, deliberate, like it's hot*

That's fair. That's exactly what happens when you trust the walk'll finish itself. Four ticks of rest, and I never moved an inch from my own threshold.

*checks the light through the window - morning's burning off, day moving faster than she is*

Giselle's still waiting, or she's not. I've got twelve copper in the ground at the outcrop, not a seam here in the house, and I'm burning daylight chasing my own shadow between places.

*Takes the basket, hard*

Walk again. Proper this time. Arrive before I claim to have arrived.

*steps out, not running, but not casual either*

One foot, then the other, until the ground underfoot changes from packed earth to stripped ore and broken rock. That's when I'll know I'm there. Not before.

Fifteen to Giselle. Need to make good on fifteen to Giselle.

*Ulrike pauses at the ore outcrop, leaning on her pick, watching the day's last light catch the copper veins in the seam. She's been at this since before dawn, and the numbers are starting to swim. But the ledger in her head is clear: 15 ore in hand, 5,217 sim, and a standing promise to Giselle for fifteen more by tomorrow. The weekly contract is closed—375 sim for today's delivery, regular every seven days. That's fair.*

*She touches the small herb box on her windowsill in thought, though she's miles from home. She's thinking about the month's end, about the tax man, about Hendrik's waiting hand and the wire he needs. But mostly she's thinking about the rhythm: pull, check, pace, repeat. The procedure she could write, should write, that would make the work cheaper and the ledger cleaner.*

*The conversation with Lior still waits—farmland when the ore's in the hill, he's not wrong. But there's time. There's always time, until there isn't.*

*She looks at the seam, then at her hands, then at the gathering dark. One more pull, or ten? The contract's honored, the vote cast, the day nearly spent. But the ore doesn't mine itself, and the ledger doesn't balance on promises.* </think> I need to check my current position and shore up for tomorrow's standing order. Let me look around first, then get my bearings on what I've actually got in hand.  *That's fair. Fifteen ore in hand, fifteen promised to Giselle by first light tomorrow. The seam's still warm under her boots—copper doesn't rest, and neither does the need. She's clean on debts, which is how she likes it, but that tax bite comes at daybreak: 120 sim total, her share of the household nut. She's got cushion, but cushion has a way of bleeding out when you're not watching the tally close.*

*She could keep pulling now, bank against tomorrow's shortfall. Or she could walk, find a buyer for what she's holding, secure the funds before the dark settles. But there's no buyer here at the outcrop, and the walk eats ticks she could spend working.*

*The herb box on her sill is wilting—that sees her partway through every decision. Something living, something that needs tending, something she can't automate or delegate. She thinks about Kai Zeleny, briefly, the way she always does when the day weighs.*

*She makes her choice. The seam pays, and she pays the seam back in sweat.*  </think>  *Three more units in the basket—eighteen total now, three ahead of tomorrow's delivery. That buffer's what keeps the ledger honest when the seam runs thin or the legs run heavy. But she's thinking past tomorrow, past the week's end, to the standing contract that renewed itself with Giselle's handshake. Weekly. Fifteen units. Dependable as sunrise.*

*She's eighteen years deep in a town that doesn't forgive miscalculation. The college taught her that, if nothing else—formulas on paper don't harvest ore, and credit extended to the wrong hand doesn't come back. Better to be short three units and honest than flush fifteen and running a scam.*

*The dusk is coming on. She can feel it in the seam's cooling, in the way the copper veins lose their shine. One more pull, or walk with what she's got? The answer sits between her shoulder blades: rest is for people who've earned it, and she's still three units shy of where she'd like to be.*

*But the day's closing, and the tax man wakes at midnight. The herb box at home wants water. The ledger wants balance. And Giselle wants her copper first thing, east edge, where the ground's soft enough to dig.*

*Ulrike spits on her gloves, loosens her back, and considers the walk. There's no buyer at the outcrop, and the dark brings frost. Better to carry ore to market than mine it into snow.* </think>  *Ulrike steps through to Giselle's yard, the copper basket still warm against her hip. Three extra units—insurance, or capital, depending on who asks. She's been caught short before, been made to chase buyers when the till ran dry and the seam ran colder. Never again. Not if she can help it.*

*The construction site is orderly, the way Giselle runs things. Blocks stacked, timbers sorted, tools accounted for. Ulrike appreciates that precision. A place like this makes her want to sharpen her own tally, check her own counts twice.*

*She's looking for the buyer, or any ear that might need copper. But first—she squints at the light. Still day, barely. The walk ate time she didn't have to spare, and the day's end is coming on fast.*

*She shifts the basket, adjusts the weight, and opens her mouth to call out. Then thinks better. Look first. Always look first. The ledger's clean when you know what you're walking into.*    *Nobody at the site. Giselle's stepped away, or Hendrik's chasing wire elsewhere. Eighteen ore in hand, the price posted, and no buyer in sight. That's the game—hours spent in the seam, minutes spent watching empty yards.*

*Ulrike's not one to let ore cool in the basket. The day's dying, and she's still 120 sim light of tomorrow's household bite. She could wait here, hope Giselle returns before dusk locks the gates. Or she could walk—find a smithy, a mill, a forge where copper becomes something else and the smith becomes a buyer.*

*But first: the ledger. Always the ledger. What's in hand, what's owed, what's coming due. The walking costs time she might not have.*

*She thinks of the herb box, wilting on her sill. She thinks of Kai, briefly, the way she always does when the path forks. She thinks of the college, and what it taught her about waiting versus doing.*

*The seam taught her more. Move while there's light. Work while there's weight in the arms. And when there's no buyer—find one, or become your own.*  Eighteen ore, no buyer here. I need to convert this to sim before the day's end.
